\section[\ar{الساعة}]{\ar{الساعة} — one word for \textquotedblleft{}hour,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}clock,\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}a moment\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:AR-C16-al-saa}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Arabic's word for \textquotedblleft{}hour\textquotedblright{} isn't native Arabic at all — it's a very old borrowing, and it still carries three meanings at once.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\ar{ساعة}} (\emph{sāʿa}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{hour}\textquotedblright{} — but also \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{clock/watch}\textquotedblright{} (as an object) and \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a while, a moment}\textquotedblright{} (as in \textquotedblleft{}wait a \emph{sāʿa}\textquotedblright{}). According to the historical linguist Theodor Nöldeke, Arabic \textbf{\ar{ساعة}} was borrowed from \textbf{Aramaic} \textbf{\ar{ش}\he{ָׁעְתָא}} (\emph{šāʿəṯā}) — the same Semitic root that gives Hebrew its word for hour, \textbf{\he{שָׁעָה}} (\emph{šāʿā}). This borrowing happened long before Islam, deep in Arabic's pre-Islamic contact with Aramaic-speaking communities — so unlike some of the religiously-tied vocabulary you've seen (like \emph{aẓ-ẓuhr}), \emph{sāʿa} is simply an old, everyday loanword, carrying no special religious weight.
\end{culture}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \ar{كم} \ar{الساعة؟} — \textquotedblleft{}how much is the hour?\textquotedblright{}}]
Arabic asks the time with \textbf{\ar{كم} \ar{الساعة؟}} (\emph{kam as-sāʿa?}), literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{how much/ how many is the hour}\textquotedblright{} — and answers with \textbf{\ar{الساعة}} + an \textbf{ordinal} number (\textquotedblleft{}the second,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the third\textquotedblright{}...):

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{الساعة} \ar{الثانية}.} — \textquotedblleft{}It is two o'clock.\textquotedblright{} (literally \textquotedblleft{}the hour {[}is{]} the second\textquotedblright{}) \textbf{\ar{الساعة} \ar{الثالثة}.} — \textquotedblleft{}It is three o'clock.\textquotedblright{} (literally \textquotedblleft{}the hour {[}is{]} the third\textquotedblright{})
\end{quote}

Be honest about the one exception: \textbf{one o'clock breaks this pattern}. You'd expect the ordinal \emph{al-ūlā} (\textquotedblleft{}the first\textquotedblright{}), but Arabic actually says \textbf{\ar{الساعة} \ar{الواحدة}} (\emph{as-sāʿa al-wāḥida}) — using \textbf{al-wāḥida}, the plain \textbf{cardinal} \textquotedblleft{}one,\textquotedblright{} not the ordinal. So the rule is \textquotedblleft{}ordinal numbers from two o'clock onward, except one o'clock, which uses the cardinal instead\textquotedblright{} — a genuine irregularity, not a typo. This is still a different grammatical shape than Spanish's \emph{la una}/\emph{las dos} or French's \emph{une heure}/\emph{deux heures}, both of which use plain cardinal numbers throughout, with no ordinal/cardinal split at all.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}sāʿa\textquotedblright{} — hour, clock, or a while, depending on context{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}kam as-sāʿa?\textquotedblright{} — what time is it?{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}as-sāʿa al-thāniya\textquotedblright{} — it is two o'clock, an ordinal number{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}as-sāʿa al-wāḥida\textquotedblright{} — it is one o'clock, the one exception, using the cardinal \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} instead{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What language did Arabic borrow \textbf{\ar{ساعة}} from, and what Hebrew word is its cousin? (\textbf{Aramaic} \emph{šāʿəṯā}; cousin of Hebrew \emph{šāʿā}.) What three things can \textbf{\ar{ساعة}} mean? (\textbf{Hour, clock/watch, and a while/moment}.) Does Arabic use cardinal or ordinal numbers to tell the time — and is there an exception? (\textbf{Ordinal} from two o'clock onward — \textquotedblleft{}the hour is the \emph{second}\textquotedblright{} — but \textbf{one o'clock is the exception}, using the cardinal \emph{al-wāḥida}, \textquotedblleft{}one,\textquotedblright{} instead of the ordinal.)
\end{tcolorbox}
